tips.title: Gland, blood, target organ
tips.body: Every hormone answer has the same three parts: **produced** in a gland, **transported in the blood**, **acts on** a target organ. Saying *travels in the blood* rather than *travels to the organ* is usually the difference between one mark and two.

tips.title: All four adrenalin effects go up
tips.body: Heart rate **up**, blood pressure **up**, blood flow to the muscles **up**, blood sugar **up**. If one of your four is a decrease, it is wrong — and *decreased heart rate* is the distractor that appears most often.

tips.title: TRH, then TSH, then thyroxine
tips.body: In alphabetical-looking order: **TRH** (hypothalamus) → **TSH** (pituitary) → **thyroxine** (thyroid). Each hormone is released by the organ before it, and the three organs come in that same order down the neck.

tips.title: Negative means opposing, not falling
tips.body: A rise triggers a response that lowers it; a fall triggers one that raises it. Writing *negative feedback lowers the level* loses the mark, because the loop works in both directions — that is the whole point of it.

tips.title: Say what switches it off
tips.body: A feedback answer is not finished until you say what happens **when the level is back to normal**. Without that step you have described a response, not a control system, and it is nearly always a separate mark.

steps.title: What the endocrine system is
steps.body:
The **endocrine system** is the body's second control system, alongside the nervous system. It works with **hormones**: chemical messengers made in **endocrine glands**, released into the **blood**, and carried to their **target organs**.

That sentence contains everything about how hormones travel, and it is worth saying in that order:

$$\textbf{produced in a gland} \rightarrow \textbf{transported in the blood} \rightarrow \textbf{acts on a target organ}$$

A hormone reaches **every** part of the body, because the blood goes everywhere. What makes it act on one organ and not another is that only the **target organ** has cells that respond to it.

**Compared with the nervous system**, hormones are **slower** to act but their effects **last longer** and are more **widespread**. A nerve impulse is electrical, travels along a neurone to one place, and is over in milliseconds; a hormone is chemical, travels in the blood to wherever the blood goes, and may act for hours.

steps.title: The pituitary: the master gland
steps.body:
The **pituitary gland**, in the brain, is often called the **master gland**, and the reason is worth understanding rather than memorising.

Most glands make a hormone that acts on a body organ. The pituitary makes hormones that act on **other glands**, telling them to release their own hormones. So it sits one level up: it controls the controllers.

You will meet this twice in this unit:

- The pituitary releases **TSH**, which tells the **thyroid** to make **thyroxine**.
- The pituitary releases **FSH** and **LH**, which act on the **ovaries** in the menstrual cycle.

That is why a question about controlling a gland usually has the pituitary in the answer somewhere.

The pituitary is itself controlled by the **hypothalamus**, a part of the brain just above it — so the chain of command runs **hypothalamus → pituitary → gland → target organ**.

**Adrenalin** is produced by the **adrenal glands**, which sit **above the kidneys**. It prepares the body for **fight or flight** — for sudden physical action.

The specification lists **four** effects, and all four are worth learning with the reason each one helps.

steps.title: Thyroxine and negative feedback
steps.body:
**Thyroxine** is produced by the **thyroid gland** in the neck, and it controls the body's **metabolic rate** — how fast the chemical reactions in cells happen.

Its level is held steady by **negative feedback**, and thyroxine is the specification's chosen example of it. Here is the loop, in the four steps the spec lists:

1. **Low** thyroxine stimulates production of **TRH** in the **hypothalamus**.
2. This causes release of **TSH** from the **pituitary gland**.
3. **TSH acts on the thyroid** to produce **thyroxine**.
4. When thyroxine levels are **normal**, thyroxine **inhibits** the release of TRH and the production of TSH.

Step 4 is what makes it *negative* feedback: the **output switches off its own production**. Without it, TSH would keep being released and thyroxine would keep rising.

The word **negative** does not mean bad or falling. It means the response **opposes** the change that triggered it: a fall triggers a rise, and a rise triggers a fall. That is how any level is held steady, and you will meet the same pattern again in blood glucose and in temperature.

steps.title: Why a constant internal environment matters
steps.body:
Many hormones exist to keep conditions inside the body **constant**, whatever is happening outside. That is **homeostasis**, and the reason it is necessary comes down to **enzymes**.

Every reaction in a cell is controlled by an enzyme, and enzymes are fussy:

- Too **cold** and the reactions are too slow to sustain life.
- Too **hot** and the enzyme **denatures** — its shape changes, the substrate no longer fits the active site, and it stops working. Unlike being too cold, this is **not reversible**.

So a body that let its temperature drift would stop working, and a body that overheated would be damaged permanently.

The same argument applies to **water**. Cells sit in a watery solution, and water moves in and out by **osmosis**. If the blood becomes too dilute, water moves **into** cells and they may **burst**; too concentrated, and water moves **out** and they **shrink**. Either way the cell cannot function.

This is why the next three topics exist: **blood glucose**, **temperature** and **water** are each held within narrow limits, and each is controlled by a negative feedback loop of exactly the kind thyroxine illustrates.

steps.title: Going deeper: the shape every control loop has
steps.body:
**One pattern, four examples.** Thyroxine, blood glucose, body temperature and water content are all controlled the same way, and seeing the shared shape turns four topics into one:

1. A **receptor** detects that the level has moved away from normal.
2. A **coordination centre** — often the hypothalamus or the pituitary — processes it.
3. An **effector** — a gland, a muscle, an organ — brings about a response.
4. The response **opposes** the original change, so the level returns towards normal.
5. As it returns, the stimulus is removed and the response **switches off**.

Step 5 is the one most answers omit, and it is usually a mark. A description that only says *the level falls* has described a response, not a **control system** — because nothing in it stops the fall continuing too far.

**Why hormones and nerves both exist.** They are suited to different jobs, and a question comparing them wants that rather than a list:

- A nerve impulse is **fast and precise**, so it is right for a **reflex** — pulling your hand from something hot.
- A hormone is **slower but longer lasting and widespread**, so it is right for something that must be sustained, like keeping the metabolic rate steady all day or running a monthly cycle.

Adrenalin sits interestingly between them: the response feels instant, but it is still a hormone, and it lasts far longer than a nerve impulse would — which is why you stay shaky for minutes after a fright.

**Precision in the wording.** Three phrasings lose marks here:

- *The hormone travels to the target organ* — true but incomplete. Say it travels **in the blood**, which reaches everywhere; the target organ is simply the one that **responds**.
- *Adrenalin gives you energy* — it does not. It **releases glucose** so that muscles can **respire** and release energy themselves.
- *Negative feedback lowers the level* — no. It **opposes the change**, whichever direction that change was in.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Hormones** are chemical messengers, made in **endocrine glands**, carried in the **blood**, acting on **target organs**.
- A hormone reaches everywhere; only the **target organ** responds to it.
- The six glands: **pituitary** (brain), **thyroid** (neck), **pancreas**, **adrenal glands** (above the kidneys), **ovaries**, **testes**.
- The **pituitary** is the **master gland**: its hormones control **other glands**.
- Compared with nerves, hormones are **slower** but **longer lasting** and more **widespread**.
- **Adrenalin** comes from the **adrenal glands** and prepares the body for **fight or flight**.
- Its four effects: **increased heart rate**, **increased blood pressure**, **increased blood flow to the muscles**, and **raised blood sugar** by the **liver changing glycogen into glucose**.
- **Thyroxine** from the **thyroid** controls **metabolic rate**.
- Its loop: low thyroxine → **TRH** (hypothalamus) → **TSH** (pituitary) → thyroxine (thyroid); normal thyroxine **inhibits** TRH and TSH.
- **Negative feedback** means the response **opposes the change** — not that the level falls.
- Constant conditions matter because **enzymes denature** when too hot and work too slowly when too cold.
- Every control loop ends by **switching itself off**, and that step is usually a mark.

questions.prompt: Explain how the level of thyroxine in the blood is controlled, naming the hormones and glands involved, and explain why this is an example of negative feedback.
questions.solution: When the level of thyroxine in the blood is low, this stimulates the production of TRH, which stands for thyrotropin releasing hormone, in the hypothalamus. TRH then causes the pituitary gland to release TSH, which stands for thyroid stimulating hormone. TSH is carried in the blood and acts on the thyroid gland, stimulating it to produce thyroxine. As a result the level of thyroxine in the blood rises back towards normal. When the level of thyroxine is normal again, the thyroxine itself inhibits the release of TRH from the hypothalamus and the production of TSH by the pituitary gland. This means less thyroxine is produced, so the level does not continue rising past normal. This is negative feedback because the response produced always opposes the original change: a fall in thyroxine brings about a rise, and a return to normal switches the response off again. Negative does not mean that the level falls, but that the change is opposed.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The loop, in four steps.**

1. **Low** thyroxine stimulates production of **TRH** in the **hypothalamus**.
2. TRH causes release of **TSH** from the **pituitary gland**.
3. **TSH acts on the thyroid gland**, which produces **thyroxine**.
4. The thyroxine level **rises back towards normal**.

**The step that completes it.** When levels are **normal**, thyroxine **inhibits** the release of TRH and the production of TSH. Production slows, so the level does not overshoot.

**Why it is negative feedback.** The response always **opposes the original change**: a fall brings about a rise, and the return to normal switches the response off again.

Note what *negative* does **not** mean. It does not mean the level falls, and it does not mean anything harmful. It means **opposing** — which is why the same word describes the control of glucose, of temperature and of water, where the change can be in either direction.

questions.prompt: Adrenalin is released when a person is frightened. Name the gland that produces it, describe its effects on the body, and explain how those effects prepare the body for sudden physical activity.
questions.solution: Adrenalin is produced by the adrenal glands, which are found just above the kidneys. It increases the heart rate, so blood is pumped around the body more quickly, and it increases blood pressure, so the blood is pushed through the vessels more forcefully. It also increases the blood flow to the muscles, so that a greater proportion of the blood goes where it will be needed. In addition it raises blood sugar levels by stimulating the liver to change glycogen into glucose. Taken together these effects mean that more oxygen and more glucose are delivered to the muscles, and delivered faster. The muscle cells can then carry out respiration at a higher rate, releasing more energy for contraction. This prepares the body for sudden physical activity, which is why the response is described as preparing for fight or flight.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The gland.** The **adrenal glands**, just **above the kidneys**.

**The four effects.**

- **Increased heart rate** — blood is pumped round faster.
- **Increased blood pressure** — blood is pushed through the vessels more forcefully.
- **Increased blood flow to the muscles** — a greater share of the blood goes where it will be needed.
- **Raised blood sugar** — adrenalin stimulates the **liver** to change **glycogen into glucose**.

**How this prepares the body.** Together, more **oxygen** and more **glucose** are delivered to the muscles, and delivered **faster**. The muscle cells can then **respire** at a higher rate, releasing more energy for contraction.

That is what *fight or flight* means: the body made ready for sudden physical action.

One piece of wording to avoid: adrenalin does **not** give the body energy. It makes **glucose available**, and the muscles release the energy themselves by respiring it.

examTechnique.body:
Name the gland, the hormone and the target organ separately. Questions often give one and ask for the others.

Say that a hormone travels in the blood, not simply that it travels to its target. The blood reaches everywhere; the target organ is the one that responds.

For adrenalin, give all four effects if the question asks what it does, and remember every one is an increase.

For thyroxine, work through the loop in order and finish with what happens when the level is normal. That last step is a separate mark.

When explaining negative feedback, say that the response opposes the change, and avoid saying it lowers the level.

If a question asks why conditions must be constant, name enzymes and say they denature when too hot.
examinerErrors: Saying hormones travel along neurones rather than in the blood.
Giving decreased heart rate as an effect of adrenalin.
Saying adrenalin gives the body energy rather than releasing glucose for respiration.
Confusing TRH with TSH, or the hypothalamus with the pituitary.
Leaving out the inhibition step when describing thyroxine control.
Saying negative feedback means the level falls.
Naming the pancreas as the source of adrenalin.
Saying enzymes are killed rather than denatured when too hot.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer treats the four control systems in this unit as one pattern rather than four sets of facts: a receptor detects a change, a coordination centre responds, an effector opposes the change, and the response then switches itself off. It always includes that last step, which most answers omit. It is precise about hormones travelling in the blood and acting only where there are cells that respond. Asked why adrenalin helps, it explains the chain through to respiration in the muscles rather than saying it gives energy. And it can say what *negative* actually means, which is what lets it apply the same reasoning to glucose and temperature later.
